extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of early-18th-century periodical essays / general literate public
extracted.subtask_description: Producing short satirical or didactic periodical essays and letters for a general public, using anecdote, moralising, and editorial apparatus (emendation, footnotes). Emphasis on domestic/social commentary and textual correction/annotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of emendation and knowledge of different readings
rubrics_metrics.description: “That useful Part of Learning which consists in Emendation, Knowledge of different Readings, and the like, is what in all Ages Persons extremely wise and learned have had in great Veneration.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat emendation and awareness of variant readings as a respected scholarly practice; display critical learning when appropriate to establish authority. The author offers to demonstrate such erudition when encouraged, implying its use as a mark of seriousness and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithful transcription of originals
rubrics_metrics.description: “I have exactly followed the Form and Spelling.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reproducing manuscripts or letters, preserve original orthography and form. Faithful transcription supports authenticity and allows readers to judge the text and variants for themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mark recovered or restored text clearly (typography)
rubrics_metrics.description: “I desire that the letter may be reprinted, and what is here recovered may be in Italic.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visually distinguish recovered, restored, or supplemented portions (e.g., italics) so readers can see what is original and what has been supplied or recovered by the editor/transcriber.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide provenance and attribution, but qualify uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: The correspondent gives pedigree claims about authorship and descent yet admits uncertainty: “I have been credibly informed ... but neither Speed, nor Baker, nor Selden, taking notice of it, I will not pretend to be positive.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give background, attribution, or provenance for reproduced material, but clearly qualify claims when evidence is imperfect; do not assert doubtful attributions as fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Announce and record emendations and corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: “According to the Emendation of the above Correspondent, the Reader is desired in the Paper of the 17th to read R. for T.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an error or variant is found, publish a clear emendation or correction and tell readers precisely how to read the earlier text. Keep a record of editorial changes for transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use footnotes to explain textual variants and provide clarifying information
rubrics_metrics.description: The issue contains footnotes that correct words and give explanatory details (e.g., variant acreage counts, orthographic corrections).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ footnotes to supply emendations, variant readings, glosses, or contextual facts that would interrupt the main text. Footnotes should clarify editorial choices and supply necessary background.

rubrics_metrics.name: End didactic pieces with explicit morals or enumerated lessons
rubrics_metrics.description: Addison closes a household complaint by listing three visible errors from his example: “First ... Secondly ... And, Lastly ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For moralizing or instructive essays, state clear, enumerated takeaways drawn from the narrative; explicit lists of lessons help readers apply the example (here: misplacing esteem, failing to distinguish life stages, letting virtues become vices by excess).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization by concrete domestic particulars to satirize excess
rubrics_metrics.description: A domestic portrait is built from detailed items — singing, painting, needlework, preserved foods, counterfeit wines, tea apparatus—to show how innocent accomplishments become obsessive expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specific, concrete domestic details (accomplishments, materials, routines, costs) to expose a character's folly or excess. Accumulated particulars make satire vivid and persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persuasive/social-advocacy letters should pair anecdote with practical recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: A correspondent recounts personal rescue by a patron and then recommends showing how small charities or patronage can be effective without expense: “It would be a worthy Work to shew what great Charities are to be done without Expence ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing for social reform or virtue, illustrate with a concrete example and propose actionable, low-cost measures readers of standing can adopt; combine personal testimony with practical counsel to persuade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of humour, repetition, and comic aside in descriptive/scene essays
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Abbey tour, the comic voice uses repeated exclamations (“a very great Man!”), curious asides, and comic misreadings to create characterization and amusement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In travel or descriptive essays, deploy comic repetition, ironic exclamation, and narrated small embarrassments or misunderstandings to build voice and entertain while conveying opinions about people or places.
